SOURCE: 2026A&A...712A.247C (Sect. 4 (inclined case): best low-diffusion fit i = 174.1 deg, Omega = 286.7 deg, relative to the nu Oct B orbit; no error bar quoted. Sect. 5: ~90% of low-diffusion solutions have i >= 170 deg; stable inclined orbits only for i > 160 deg.): mutual inclination 174.1 deg. The paper's words: 'Stable fits to all radial velocity data require the planetary orbit to be retrograde and practically coplanar.' (2025Natur.641..866C, Abstract (Nature; full text paywalled, abstract read on nature.com)). Ramm et al. 2021 (MNRAS 502, 2793) is an activity analysis; it defines 'type-2 retrograde' = retrograde relative to the two stellar orbits and gives no new mutual-inclination value (its Table 2 summarises R09/R16/Gozdziewski 2013 and notes Quarles 2012 and Gozdziewski 2013 favour a coplanar orbit 'which R16 could not confirm'). Sky-plane I1 = 108.2 deg is NOT itself the retrograde evidence; the retrograde statement is about the mutual inclination with the binary. Signor et al. 2026 bibcode first-author initial is 'C' (Cefali Signor). Planet's secondary B is a white dwarf (Cheng et al. 2025).

SOURCE: 2022AJ....164...93C (Sect. 5.5 (Mutual Inclination Angle), Eq. 13; abstract. Alternative node (Omega_Ab + 180) gives 67 deg but is unstable within a few thousand yr (Sect. 5.6). No uncertainty quoted for Phi.): mutual inclination 148 deg. The paper's words: 'The planetary and binary orbits are found to be in a retrograde configuration' (2022AJ....164...93C, Abstract; also Sect. 6: 'consistent with both orbits being retrograde'). The binary's i > 90 deg in the sky frame only means clockwise on the sky; the retrograde claim rests on the 148 deg mutual inclination. Searches (SIMBAD refs, web) found no later paper confirming or disputing the planet or the angle.

Planet node unknown, so no true mutual inclination. 'consistent with the assumption of a well-aligned, coplanar system' (2019A&A...625A..59J).

UNCLEAR or WEAK (weak), drawn prograde: Single point value 113.9 deg (just over the 110 deg line; the paper itself calls it 'nearly perpendicular'). It is computed from the planet's sky inclination and node I1 = 5.7 deg, Omega1 = 37.5 deg adopted from the re-reduced Hipparcos intermediate data of Reffert & Quirrenbach 2011 (2011A&A...527A.140R), an alternative I1 = 173.1 deg, Omega1 = 356.1 deg also being listed, with the binary's I2/Omega2 from Neuhauser et al. 2007. No error propagated; the Hipparcos detection of a ~2 au planet's reflex orbit is marginal. Treat as a weak hint of a near-polar/retrograde orbit, not a measurement. Angle 113.9 deg (2022AJ....164..177H, Sect. 2.2 (Eq. 2): i_mut = 113.9 deg for I1 = 5.7 deg; no uncertainty quoted). 'occupies a nearly perpendicular planetary orbit relative to the binary' (2022AJ....164..177H).

cells.note: UNCLEAR or WEAK (weak), drawn prograde: Unconfirmed JWST/MIRI candidate (one sighting plus non-detections). cells.note: UNCLEAR or WEAK (weak), drawn prograde: Unconfirmed GRAVITY astrometric candidate (156 d, ~36 Earth masses). Fit is degenerate among four solutions (two host stars x two nodes); the prograde ones are shown as 'favored from a dynamical point of view' (Sect. 4, orbit fitting). Delta i is a difference of sky inclinations, not a full 3D angle. Angle 30 deg (2024A&A...685L...9G, Sect. 5: Delta i ~ 30 +/- 10 deg between the planet orbit (i_p ~ 90 deg, Table 2) and the binary/stellar equatorial planes). 'the planetary orbit plane has a moderate-to-high inclination of i > 30 deg with respect to the stellar pair' (2024A&A...685L...9G).

UNCLEAR or WEAK (weak), drawn prograde: Unconfirmed velocity-anomaly candidate. arXiv:2609.32893 (Worlds Next Door V, Sect. 3/Fig. 3-4) only maps which mutual inclinations relative to the 61 Cyg AB orbit are dynamically stable: near-polar (~80-100 deg) orbits are entirely unstable; prograde and retrograde both allowed. No measured angle.

sp_column_rows: Measured where a paper measured it: the spin-orbit angle (Rossiter-McLaughlin / Doppler tomography; TEPCat and the papers, data/orbit_direction/research/spin.json) or the orbit against a binary companion, a host binary or the other planets (astrometry, imaging; research/orbits.json). Written '<Direction> (vs <reference>; <angle>)'. Every other planet reads 'Prograde (assumed)' -- the model's default, not a measurement (no border, as the Data Sparse spin-orbit cells).

High where the paper states polar/retrograde (plain cell, SOURCE note); a direction classified from a published angle by this project's thresholds (prograde < 70 deg, polar 70-110, retrograde > 110; psi where known, else |lambda|) is boxed orange with an INFERRED note. Weak or ambiguous results stay 'assumed', with a note saying what is known.

Why: nu Oct A b orbits retrograde against its binary (Ramm et al. 2009/2021; Cheng et al. 2025, Nature 641, 866) but was drawn prograde -- every catalog planet was drawn coplanar and prograde. Each planet on both tabs was checked for a measured or well-evidenced polar or retrograde orbit.

Polar or retrograde: GJ 436 b: Polar (vs stellar spin; ψ 103°); GJ 3470 b: Polar (vs stellar spin; ψ 95°); GJ 3090 b: Retrograde (vs stellar spin; ψ 136°); nu Oct A b: Retrograde (vs binary orbit; 174°); GJ 896 A b: Retrograde (vs binary orbit; 148°); VHS J125601.92-125723.9 b: Retrograde (vs host binary orbit; 118°); GJ 523 b: Polar (vs stellar spin; ψ ≥ 71°).

Against the star's spin (polar/retrograde) the viewer tilts the star's spin axis by the angle; against a binary companion it draws the planet going round the other way, the star's axis assumed (dashed) to follow the binary. Everything else reads 'Prograde (assumed)'.
Spin-orbit column corrected: GJ 3470 b to the published psi = 95 +9/-8 (was arXiv v1's 97 +16/-11); GJ 3090 b filled, psi = 136 +24/-18 (Carteret et al. 2026).

Not drawn as misaligned, weak or ambiguous: gam Cep b (113.9 deg vs binary, marginal Hipparcos inclination), 14 Her b-c (32 or 145 deg), pi Men b-c (52-129 deg, sense unknown), AU Mic c (aligned or polar), alf Cen A b; lower bounds only for GJ 504 b, 51 Eri b, CD-35 2722 b.
